title: Allowance for Kids by Age: How Much + Free Chart
meta_description: A dad of four shares a real allowance-by-age model: ~$5/week starting at 5-6, teens on a $75/month job plan, plus a free chore-and-money chart.
h1: Allowance for Kids by Age: How Much and How to Set It Up
intro: If you've ever stood in the kitchen wondering "how much allowance is actually right for a six-year-old versus a fifteen-year-old?" — you're in the right place. We're the SproutChores family: I'm Andrew, a dad of four (ages 9 to 18), and over the years my wife and I have run allowance across every age band, toddler through teen. We've also fostered three young kids, which taught us a lot about how much structure and consistency matter. This guide lays out the exact age-based model we use, why we keep everyday family chores unpaid, and how to set it all up without turning your home into a tip-jar economy. There's a free chore-and-money chart at the bottom — but a heads-up: in our house that chart is a tracking tool for us as parents, not a sticker gimmick to bribe the kids.

sections.heading: How Much Allowance by Age (Our Real Breakdown)
sections.body:
We don't price chores per task. Allowance in our house is a small base amount tied to overall follow-through — quality of work, staying on track, and attitude — not a transaction for each thing done. Here's how it scales by age:

- Ages 2-4 (toddlers): No allowance. The focus is self-care (getting dressed, brushing teeth, cleaning up their own messes) and letting them "help" without requiring it. There's nothing to pay for yet.
- Ages 5-6 (allowance begins): About $5/week. This is when kids join the family chore chart, and the small allowance starts alongside it — but it's gated on quality, consistency, and a good attitude, not handed out automatically.
- Ages 6-10: Still in the ~$5/week range, scaling modestly as they grow. Complexity rises here — dishes, helping with cooking, trash, outdoor and repair work. They're expected to do their jobs well and without constant reminders before allowance holds steady.
- Ages 11-12 (pre-teen): A step up from the early-elementary amount as responsibilities and trust grow. We raise it as proficiency rises, not just because a birthday happened.
- Teens (13+): Roughly $75/month on a job-style arrangement (more on this below). At this stage we drop the family chore chart entirely.

The through-line: amounts scale with maturity and proven reliability, not with how many boxes got checked on a given day.

sections.heading: Should Allowance Be Tied to Chores? (Why We Keep Them Separate)
sections.body:
This is the question every parent wrestles with, and our answer is a deliberate one: everyday family chores are unpaid. We found that framing chores as "we all contribute" — responsibilities we owe each other as a family unit — works far better than paying per task. The moment a kid can opt out by forgoing a dollar, you've taught them that contributing is optional. We don't want that.

So where does the money fit? Allowance exists, but it's a base tied to overall behavior and reliability, not a per-chore price list. A child can do their normal jobs and earn their weekly allowance; the allowance reflects whether they showed up consistently, did the work well, and kept a reasonable attitude — not whether they "completed transaction X."

We also keep rewards and screen-time out of the chore equation. We don't make our kids work for screen time or fun. Screen-time removal is a consequence for genuine bad behavior, not a chore currency. For the younger ones, our main reward is a dollar-store "treasure chest" they can pick from once or twice a week when work was done well and with a good attitude — cheap enough that it stays a treat, not a paycheck. Keeping these layers separate (chores, allowance, rewards) is what stops the whole system from collapsing into bribery.

sections.heading: The Teen Years: Allowance Becomes a Job
sections.body:
Teens are the hardest age to keep on a chore chart — honestly, near-impossible to enforce. We've now raised two through the teen years (our 15- and 18-year-olds) with two more approaching, and the thing that finally clicked was to stop treating it like a chart and start treating it like a job with pay.

Here's the arrangement: our teens get about $75/month. The chore chart is gone. In exchange for that money, we reserve the right to ask them for agreed-upon tasks ahead of time — babysitting their younger siblings, cleaning, cooking — and those tasks aren't tracked on a chart. If they miss or forget tasks, their income gets reduced at the end of the month. If non-follow-through continues, the money pauses until they've shown a couple of weeks of consistency to earn it back.

The key detail that keeps them motivated: this money is for wants, not needs. We cover their needs. The $75 is for the Starbucks run with friends, the extras. Because it funds the stuff they actually care about, the natural consequence of losing it does the motivating for us — no nagging required.

sections.heading: How to Set Up Allowance by Age in Your Home
sections.body:
A few practical steps from what's worked for us:

1. Pick a start age and a base amount. We begin around 5-6 with roughly $5/week, timed to when kids join the family chore chart. Choose what fits your budget — the exact number matters less than the consistency.
2. Decide your gates up front. We pay on quality, consistency, and attitude. Tell your kids plainly what earns the full allowance and what reduces it, so it never feels arbitrary.
3. Keep everyday chores unpaid. Make clear that basic contributions (their room, shared spaces, helping out) are simply part of being in the family. Allowance rides on top of that as a reflection of overall follow-through.
4. Plan the teen transition. Somewhere in the early teens, retire the chart and switch to the monthly job-style model with month-end adjustments. It respects their growing independence and is far more enforceable.
5. Use a chart as YOUR tracking tool, not their motivator. We track on paper and tape things up where the work actually happens — kids need it visible. But the chart's real job is to let us see how each kid is doing and decide when to step in. The motivation comes from the expectation and the family structure, not from the chart itself.

If you want a head start, our free chore-and-money chart includes a money-value column and an age-based layout built around exactly this model. Pair it with our chore chart with money guide and our chore-app round-up if you want to compare paper versus app tracking.

faq.q: What age should kids start getting an allowance?
faq.a: In our house allowance starts around age 5-6, the same time kids join the family chore chart. Before that (ages 2-4), the focus is on self-care like dressing and brushing teeth — there's nothing to pay for yet. We begin with about $5/week, gated on quality, consistency, and attitude rather than handed out automatically.

faq.q: How much allowance should I give by age?
faq.a: We use roughly $5/week starting at 5-6 and scale it up modestly through the elementary years as kids grow and prove reliable. Pre-teens get a small step up. Teens move to a different model entirely — about $75/month on a job-style arrangement, where the chore chart is dropped and money is adjusted at month-end based on follow-through.

faq.q: Should allowance be tied to chores?
faq.a: We keep everyday family chores unpaid, on purpose. Chores are framed as "we all contribute," not as paid transactions — so a kid can't opt out by skipping the money. Allowance still exists, but it's a base amount tied to overall quality, consistency, and attitude, not a per-task price. We also keep rewards and screen-time completely separate from chores.

faq.q: How do allowances work for teenagers?
faq.a: For teens we treat it like a job with pay: about $75/month, no chore chart. The money comes with the expectation that we can ask for agreed-upon tasks ahead of time — babysitting, cooking, cleaning. Missed or forgotten tasks reduce their income at month-end, and ongoing non-follow-through pauses it until they show a couple weeks of consistency. The money funds wants, not needs, which keeps them motivated.
